project: A municipal sports complex: bookings with setup and teardown buffers that may never overlap.

steps.title: The complex, as a day you can look at
steps.scene: Four grounds, opening hours that differ on Sundays, and six event types each with its own setup and teardown. All of it lives on a wall planner, in pencil.
steps.build: Load grounds, hours, event types and their buffers once before the server listens, from `@ConfigurationProperties`, and serve a day that can be read as blocks and the shadows around them — the shadow derived from the event type, never stored as a second booking somebody has to remember to move.
steps.follows: Nothing can be requested, confirmed or moved until the complex exists.

story.want: see a ground's day as blocks and the setup and teardown around them
story.so: I can see the real shape of the day, not just the matches

steps.summary: The app starts with four grounds, their opening hours and six event types with buffers loaded once, and answers a day as blocks with the shadows around them.

rules: The shadow is computed on read from the booking's event type: `groundHeldFrom = from − setup`, `groundHeldTo = to + teardown`. No column stores it.

steps.title: A club asks for a slot
steps.scene: Rafi calls Deepa for Saturday, two till five. He does not say that his ground staff arrive at twenty past one, because on the planner that has never mattered.
steps.build: A request endpoint taking an interval and an event type through a record DTO with Bean Validation (`@Valid`, `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`), answering 201 through `ResponseEntity` — and separating a malformed interval (400 with field detail) from one that ends before it starts or falls outside the ground's hours (400).
steps.follows: The day is readable; this is the first thing that changes it, so validation lives here.

story.want: request a slot by interval and event type
story.so: my booking carries the setup time my ground staff actually need

steps.summary: A club requests a slot by ground, interval and event type and gets a `requested` booking back; an impossible interval is refused differently from a malformed body.

codes: the body fails validation; `errors[]` names each field
`to` is not after `from`, or the interval crosses the ground's opening hours; `opens`/`closes` say the hours
no such ground at this venue
no such booking at this venue

data: bookings(id, venue_id, ground_id, event_type_id, club_name, from_at, to_at, state requested|confirmed|cancelled|expired, requested_at, hold_until); settings HOLD_HOURS (24)
rules: `from` and `to` must parse, `to` > `from`, `from` not before the injected clock's now (nobody books the past), both on the same date, and the *shadow* must lie within the ground's hours for that weekday — everything after parsing is 400 bad-interval (valid body, impossible request).
Minimum interval 30 minutes, maximum 12 hours — validation.
`holdUntil` = requested_at + HOLD_HOURS from the injected clock. No overlap check yet.

The request is a record DTO with Bean Validation (`@Valid`, `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`); a malformed body and a broken rule both answer 400 and are told apart by `type` in the body, tested separately. Each entry of `errors[]` is `{field, message}`; a `from` Jackson cannot read is still a 400 whose `errors[]` names the field. The length bounds (30 minutes to 12 hours) span two fields, so the service checks them and answers the same 400 /errors/validation. `requestedAt`, `holdUntil` and the not-in-the-past rule read a `java.time.Clock` bean; the grader puts its own `Clock` in its place.

done: Endpoint with all responses; booking row written; hold computed; shadow-within-hours tested.

steps.title: Confirm, cancel, and the hour that has already gone
steps.scene: A club cancels a slot that started twenty minutes ago and expects it back on the planner as free. The same afternoon, Sabu tries to confirm a slot that has already begun.
steps.build: Confirm and cancel as real transitions, with the rules that depend on the current time — you cannot confirm a slot that has begun, you cannot cancel one that is over — read from an injected `Clock` bean so a test can move time instead of waiting.
steps.follows: Requests exist; this is what resolves them. The injected `Clock` bean is what every time rule is tested through.

story.want: confirm and cancel bookings with the rules about time already passed
story.so: nobody cancels a slot that has already started and expects it back

steps.summary: Confirm and cancel are real transitions with rules that depend on the injected clock.

codes: the interval has begun; it can no longer be confirmed or moved
a cancelled booking cannot be confirmed or moved; request a new one
no such booking at this venue
cancelled; `late` is true when the interval had begun
the interval has ended; it can no longer be cancelled
no such booking at this venue

data: bookings gains confirmed_at, cancelled_at, late_cancel bool
rules: Confirm requires state requested and now < from. Cancel requires state requested or confirmed and now < to; if now ≥ from it is a late cancel — allowed and flagged `late`; the remainder of the slot is free from now, and since nobody can book the past nothing else needs protecting.
All `now` comparisons use the injected clock.
`java.time.Clock` bean; `Clock.fixed` in tests.
The service takes `Clock` (and the repository) by constructor injection — no field injection, no `Instant.now()` outside the clock — so a test constructs it with `Clock.fixed`.
ac_user: a club cancels a slot that started twenty minutes ago
it is marked cancelled late — the strip does not show the hour as free
Sabu confirms a slot that has begun
done: Both transitions with all refusals under a fixed clock; late flag stored.

try.do: Request a slot on the Book screen and open its booking card (the booking number in the green panel, or its block on The day). Press Confirm, then Confirm again. Request another slot, open it and press Cancel.
try.see: Confirm answers 200 with `confirmedAt`; a second Confirm is 409 already-confirmed. Cancel before the start answers `late: false`, and the block on The day turns grey. Once the interval has begun, Confirm is 409 already-started and Cancel is 200 with `late: true` — the card says "cancelled late" and the strip keeps the block, shown as cancelled, rather than showing the hour as free. After the interval has ended Cancel is 409 already-over. Every `now` is the injected `Clock` bean; a test swaps it for a fixed one, since the page runs on today's time.

steps.title: The refusals, once the shadows are counted
steps.scene: Two clubs are on the planner back to back at four o'clock. On paper they do not overlap. In reality one is clearing the ground while the other is putting up nets on it. And a booking a club cancelled last week must not come back just because someone presses confirm.
steps.build: Refuse an overlap once buffers are counted on both sides, and refuse a cancelled booking being reconfirmed — each with its own code, thrown from a `@Service` and mapped by `@RestControllerAdvice`, never handled in a controller.
steps.follows: The happy path is built. The buffered overlap is the whole point of this project, and it becomes the first row of its rule table.

story.want: be refused an overlap once buffers are counted on both sides
story.so: two clubs never arrive at the same ground on the same afternoon

steps.summary: Overlap is refused once buffers are counted on both sides, and a cancelled booking cannot be reconfirmed — each with its own code, raised from the service.

codes: the shadow (interval plus buffers) clashes with another booking's shadow; `clashesWith` lists booking ids and their held ranges
the shadow clashes with nothing live on that ground
a cancelled booking cannot be confirmed or moved; request a new one
the shadow (interval plus buffers) clashes with another booking's shadow; `clashesWith` lists booking ids and their held ranges

rules: Live bookings are requested (not past holdUntil) and confirmed. A new request clashes if its shadow intersects any live booking's shadow on the same ground: `held_from_new < held_to_other AND held_from_other < held_to_new`.
Confirm re-runs the check (a competing request may have been confirmed since).
Domain refusals are exceptions (Overlap, Cancelled, AlreadyStarted, AlreadyOver) raised in the service and mapped by one handler.

Exceptions are thrown from a `@Service` and mapped once in a `@RestControllerAdvice`; no `try/catch` that builds a response inside a controller. A `@WebMvcTest` on the booking controller, with the service replaced by a `@MockitoBean`, proves the mapping without starting the database.
ac_user: refused: on paper they do not overlap, with buffers they do — and she is told which booking
ac_api: request 17:10–19:00 held from 16:30, exactly where A's shadow ends (half-open: touching shadows do not clash)
type, title, status, detail, instance, named fields; no trace
done: Overlap on shadows both sides; reconfirm refused; one handler; a test per refusal.

try.do: Request ground A, League match, From 14:00, To 16:00 on a Saturday. Then request the same ground and day From 16:00, To 18:00. Then From 17:10, To 19:00. Cancel a booking on its card and press Confirm on it.
try.see: On paper 14:00-16:00 and 16:00-18:00 do not touch; with buffers the first is held to 16:30 and the second from 15:20, so the second is 409 overlap with `clashesWith` naming the first booking and its held range — The day marks the two shadows in red. 17:10-19:00 is held from 16:30 exactly and is 201: the predicate is half-open. Confirming a cancelled booking is 409 cancelled. Every refusal is thrown from a `@Service` and mapped by the one `@RestControllerAdvice`; the table under the form lists each one the API documents.

steps.title: Moving a booking without breaking the day
steps.scene: Rafi asks to shift Saturday an hour later. Sabu erases the pencil mark, redraws it, and only then notices the school sports day.
steps.build: A move that re-checks the whole interval — including both buffers — inside one `@Transactional` boundary, so a booking is never briefly in two places or briefly in none.
steps.follows: What may not overlap is settled; a move is the first operation that could break it in the middle of itself.

story.want: move my booking and have the whole interval re-checked
story.so: a change of time cannot quietly create a clash

steps.summary: A move re-checks the whole new interval including both buffers, in one transaction — never briefly in two places or none.

try.do: Open a booking card (click its block on The day), then use the Move form on the card: first into a clash with the next booking on that ground, then into a free hour.

steps.title: A planner nobody can erase
steps.scene: Two clubs arrive at the same ground. The planner shows one booking, cleanly written, and nobody can say what was rubbed out.
steps.build: An append-only log written through `JdbcClient`: one row per transition — requested, confirmed, moved, cancelled — written in the same `@Transactional` boundary as the change, never updated and never deleted.
steps.follows: A move rewrites history; this is what stops it being rewritten silently, and the log that proves nothing overlapped.

story.want: see every request, confirmation, move and cancellation in a record nobody can erase
story.so: a disputed Saturday has one account of what happened

steps.summary: Every transition is written to an append-only log in the same transaction, readable per booking.

codes: no such booking at this venue

data: events(id, venue_id, booking_id, kind requested|confirmed|moved|cancelled|expired|charged|invoiced|rechecked, at, actor_id, data json) — insert only; immutability enforced and tested
rules: Written in the same transaction; a rolled-back move leaves no `moved` event.
Events carry ids, intervals and facts — never the club's name, phone or email.
The booking's `events` are the only history shown.

Event rows are inserted through `JdbcClient` inside the same `@Transactional` boundary as the change they record; the events repository has an insert and a read and nothing else, so nothing can update them.

ac_api: one `moved` event with old and new intervals
done: Every transition logged in-transaction; immutability enforced; GET returns ordered events.

try.do: Open a booking you requested, confirmed, moved and cancelled.

steps.title: One file becomes an app
steps.scene: A club with a website asks whether it can request slots directly instead of telephoning Deepa.
steps.build: Packages by feature for grounds, bookings and moves; one `@RestControllerAdvice` so every refusal has the same shape; tags, summaries and documented errors, so the springdoc Swagger UI is something a club's developer could follow.
steps.follows: The rules so far have piled into one module. The problem+json shape is settled here.

story.so: clubs can request slots online without guessing what an error means

steps.summary: Routers for grounds, bookings and moves, one error shape, and docs a club's developer can build against.

codes: every endpoint with summary, tag (grounds, bookings, moves) and documented errors
every 4xx in the codes tables on its endpoint

rules: Packages by feature: `ground`, `booking`, `move`, each controller/service/repository; controllers hold no rules, and services import nothing from the web layer (no `ResponseEntity`, no Spring web or servlet types).
One handler for every error class.
Every endpoint documents its errors with an example.
Every endpoint has `@Tag` and `@Operation`, and every refusal it can give an `@ApiResponse` with a problem+json `@ExampleObject`; springdoc builds the Swagger UI from them; controllers hold no rules.

steps.title: The rule table, and then the rule changes
steps.scene: The city decides buffers should differ by event type: twenty minutes for a practice session, two hours for a sports day.
steps.build: A `@ParameterizedTest` table driven from `@CsvFileSource` of every refusal the planner can give, run through MockMvc on the whole app against a fixed `Clock` — then change the buffers (a uniform 40/30 table against each event type's own) and watch which rows move.
steps.follows: The refusals exist and time can be moved, so the buffer rule can be changed with evidence rather than hope.

story.want: set buffers per event type and see exactly which rules moved
story.so: a policy change does not quietly permit a clash

steps.summary: A parametrised rule table covers every refusal, then the buffers change - a uniform table against each type's own - and only the buffer rows move.
data: event_types.setup_minutes/teardown_minutes are the source of every buffer (loaded with the seed); the table also runs against a uniform 40/30 table, and there is no uniform-buffer setting
rules: The table: one row per case — ok / to before from / outside hours / shadow outside hours / overlap on the left buffer / overlap on the right buffer / back-to-back with buffers that just fit / confirm started / cancel over / late cancel / reconfirm cancelled / move into clash / move ok.
`@CsvFileSource`; the test drives the whole app through MockMvc (`@SpringBootTest` with `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`) with a fixed `Clock` bean.
Changing practice to 20/20 and school_day to 120/120 moves exactly the rows tagged `buffer`.

The table is one `@ParameterizedTest` with `@CsvFileSource`, driven through MockMvc on the whole app (`@SpringBootTest` with `@AutoConfigureMockMvc`, because the rows need the database) with a fixed `Clock` bean; the buffer change is made in the event_types rows the test starts from.

steps.title: It runs on the office machine
steps.scene: Deepa's office has one PC that also runs the property tax software. Nobody is installing Java on it.
steps.build: A Dockerfile that builds the Spring Boot jar in a first stage and runs it on an Eclipse Temurin JRE base, an image built and run with a mapped port, and `server.address` bound to 0.0.0.0 (from `HOST`) so Sabu's tablet at the gate can reach it.
steps.follows: The app is finished and tested; this is the first day it leaves your laptop.

story.want: run the planner from a single image on the office machine
story.so: I do not need a developer to start it

steps.summary: The app builds into an image and runs in a container on the office PC, reachable from Sabu's gate tablet.
rules: Dockerfile in two stages: the jar is built in a first stage (`eclipse-temurin:21-jdk` running the Maven Wrapper) and copied into `eclipse-temurin:21-jre`; `EXPOSE 8080`, `ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar`; `server.address=0.0.0.0`. The machine that builds the image needs Docker and nothing else.
Two commands; README shows them.
The tablet reaches the day strip on the PC's IP:8080.

steps.title: It survives being switched off
steps.scene: The office PC is restarted for an update and Saturday's bookings are gone on a Friday afternoon.
steps.build: A volume for the H2 file, configuration through env vars and Spring relaxed binding rather than baked into the image, a .dockerignore, logs to stdout — and the README that walks one booking from request to the gate being unlocked.
steps.follows: The image ran once; this makes it something the municipal office can be handed.

story.so: an overnight update is not a Friday afternoon emergency
